reason: The text narrates Amnon, a member of the elite (son of King David), committing morally heinous acts—deception and rape of his sister Tamar. These actions are explicitly condemned within the narrative as 'foolish' (navala) and contrary to Israeli norms. Tamar, of lower status, is portrayed as morally righteous in her resistance and plea. The narrative exposes moral corruption within the elite class rather than demonstrating their inherent superiority. King David, though elite, is shown as ineffectual in addressing the crime, and Absalom's hatred of Amnon stems from moral outrage. The text suggests social position does not confer moral superiority, and elite status may even enable moral transgression.
